title: The AI-designed USB-C LTE Modem is built, and it makes calls
content:
Comments

abijahkaj · Nov 28, 2026

A month ago I posted this board here: a 4-layer USB-C LTE modem (Quectel EC25 + an RP2040 as a USB sound card) that Koppar designed from a one-page spec. A few people said it would never get built, or wouldn't work if it did.

It's built, and it works. On the bench:

- registers on 4G (bands 3 and 20) on a French SIM, both antennas on U.FL

- texts in and out, long multi-part ones included

- calls placed and answered, two-way audio through the Mac's mic and speakers via the RP2040 sound card

- USB hub at 480 Mb/s, the 3.8 V rail at 3.81 V under the module's load

Bring-up wasn't all smooth: I soldered the EC25 by hand, and both boards needed a second pass, and the first batch shipped without the recovery pads, so getting into the RP2040 bootloader meant tweezers on the flash chip. It's all in the post and in REV-C.md.

Unexpected bit: Esuna Labs put this board in RealPCB, their benchmark of AI agents doing PCB layout (https://github.com/esunalabs/realpcb, task pcb-6b4cc11f313f). Each agent gets the parts unplaced and two hours in KiCad, and is graded against the released layout, which is our rev B. Of the six frontier models they ran on it, only Fable 5.2 came within margin. GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, Sonnet, Haiku and Grok didn't.

Repo with the KiCad files, REVIEW.md, the firmware and a macOS menu-bar app for calls and texts: https://github.com/Koppar-AI/koppar-lte-modem

lefra · Nov 28, 2026

The Quectel EC25 has all the RF stuff already done. It exposes a serial-over-USB port, and you need to wire up a power supply and an antenna to it. Copy-paste what's in the datasheet and it should work.

Onve this is plugged to a USB port, configure ppp correctly and point it to the serial port and you get an LTE connection.

Also "it works" doesn't mean that EMI was correctly handled, this needs to go through certification (CE/RED for EU, FCC for US) to be sure (and to be legally sold).

just_mc · Nov 28, 2026

I've been doing a lot of work in this area over the last few weeks. I started out using Koppar and the initial results were quite impressive. However, as the board gets more complicated, it will fall over pretty quickly. I have had good success using Claude Opus with the KiCAD Routing Tools placer and router. From what I have seen, routing is pretty strong, but placement is fairly weak. I had Claude build some tools to perform basic analysis on the floorplan fed to the placer and this improved the outcome quite a bit. Also, I put quite a bit of effort into having Claude perform simulations using ngspice and OpenEMS and this feedback loop seems to have provided a great deal of value. I just ordered the first round of boards, so in a few weeks we will see how it all turned out.

eqvinox · Nov 28, 2026

This isn't a LTE modem; the LTE modem is the Quectel EC25-EUX. This is a relatively simple carrier board.

This is a single buck, a RP2040, and soldering down a module.

Granted, power management is an important part, especially due to the higher integration of chips & modules ⇒ lowering number of other things in the design, but also sometimes additional power rails ⇒ increase of relative quota of power management.

…so where are the power rail scope measurements? And why are the inductor and capacitors so physically large? And why didn't the design go with the TI recommended newer TPS563203?

I'll even forgo the RF validation on the antenna traces given how short they are… (not necessarily a good idea tbh)

[ed.: oof, I didn't see that antenna trace right next to the power inductor. That's… not a good idea. I'm taking back that forgo on the RF validation. How much stray 580kHz is getting injected into that antenna connection?]

abijahkaj · Nov 28, 2026

It's not a breakout board, it's a finished device: one USB-C cable in, and the computer sees a network adapter, the AT ports and a USB sound card carrying the call audio (the module's PCM, level-shifted into an RP2040). Plus the hub, the 3.8 V supply for the 2 A bursts, SIM, 50 Ω feeds, LEDs, firmware and a Mac app.

The LTE itself is Quectel's, as it is in every phone that uses a module.

here's the repo: https://github.com/Koppar-AI/koppar-lte-modem
